key_insight: Creep cracking in metals transitions from trans-granular to inter-granular dominance as stress decreases, governed by a stress-dependent competition between grain-boundary cavitation and slip-induced intragranular cracking.
engineering_relevance: The framework links microscale damage mechanisms to rupture life and ductility, helping engineers predict high-temperature creep failure modes and design more damage-resistant alloys and components.
method: Unified crystal plasticity-fracture model coupling crystal plasticity, grain-boundary cavitation, and crystallographic crack propagation
Explicit polycrystalline microstructure simulation to resolve grain-boundary and grain-interior damage evolution
Stress-level study of cracking transitions from high-stress trans-granular damage to low-stress inter-granular fracture
evidence_signal: The abstract reports microscale computations showing distinct damage localization and crack-path evolution across stress levels, with corresponding changes in rupture ductility and creep life.
watch_item: Because the approach relies on detailed microstructural modeling and fracture laws, calibration and transferability to different alloys, temperatures, and loading histories may require significant validation.
paper_title: Mechanistic transition between inter- and trans-granular creep cracking via a unified crystal plasticity-fracture framework
